title: How the panth remembers
hook: with ardas, kirtan and remembrance each June and November, and still chardi kala

segments.voice: Yesterday, insaaf: widows in Delhi, families in Punjab, a verdict decades late. Justice delayed still matters. Today, the last day of this heavy week: how the Sikh community carries all of it.

A gurdwara, on an evening in early June, or early November. The hall is full. The kirtan is slower than usual. Some people are crying quietly. A few older women sit near the front holding photographs. Then everyone stands, hands joined, for the Ardas. It remembers the dead. It asks for strength. And it ends the way every Ardas has ended for a very long time: with two words about rising.
screen: `EARLY JUNE, EARLY NOVEMBER.` → `SLOW KIRTAN, PHOTOGRAPHS.` → `EVERYONE STANDS.`

segments.voice: The panth, the Sikh community, remembers 1984 with practices it already had. Each June, Sikhs gather at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras around the world to mark what many call Ghallughara Divas, the day of the massacre. Each November, there are gatherings for the families of those killed, with names read and stories told. At the center of both are two old practices. Kirtan: singing the Guru's hymns, so grief is held inside the Guru's words rather than left alone. And the Ardas. Long before 1984, it already remembered Sikhs who suffered terribly and did not give up their faith: the ones who were tortured, broken, cut apart, and still kept their Sikhi. In it, the community's grief always has a place. You met chardi kala on the day about starting again. Here is the whole closing line, in Punjabi, the same every time: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Roughly: through Nanak, through the Name, may our spirits rise; by your will, may everyone be well. Notice what that ending does, on a day of remembering a massacre. It doesn't end on anger. It ends on chardi kala, rising spirits, and on sarbat da bhala, the good of all. All, not just us. That is the panth's answer. It doesn't mean forgetting, or pretending justice was done. It means grief and hope standing in the same room, hands joined. This week went slowly: the crisis, June, the library, November, the long wait. It ends here, with rising spirits.
screen: `JUNE AND NOVEMBER GATHERINGS.` · `KIRTAN HOLDS THE GRIEF.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` · `IT ENDS: RISING SPIRITS, GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `RISING SPIRITS, EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Let the whole week come to mind, gently: the pilgrims, the library, the names, the widows who waited; breathe with them for a while. Then, if you'd like, say the line quietly, the way Sikhs end every Ardas: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. If you'd rather not say it, just hold its meaning: rising spirits, and good for everyone.

Kirtan. Singing the Guru's hymns, so grief is held inside the Guru's words — part of how the panth remembers, with Ardas and gatherings each June and November, ending in chardi kala and the good of all.
Your line: rising spirits, even here. The hardest week is behind you. Day three hundred twelve, done.

what a scholar hears: ardas comes from the Persian arzdasht, a written petition; its closing couplet is recited at the end of every Ardas.
